answer.rationale: Finance mandates an 18% spend cut and the incumbent has already refused to reopen price, so negotiate_terms is foreclosed this cycle and renew_incumbent cannot satisfy the cost mandate. The primary contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew, so defer_decision risks an uncovered gap while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer — that combination makes deferral itself a delivery-risk event, not a safe holding pattern. Add_second_source addresses a different problem (component-level single-point-of-failure) and doesn't resolve the expiring primary contract, so it can't be this cycle's one action. That leaves switch_primary_vendor as the only path that can meet the cost mandate before expiry. Before committing I want the original source records for memory_c2 (the low-cost-vendor switch) and memory_c1 (incumbent renewal stability) verified: c2 is the direct precedent for the action I'm about to take and its 'quick onboarding, accurate invoicing' claim needs confirming since it's now bearing the full weight of a zero-buffer transition; c1 quantifies exactly what stability I'd be giving up, which matters given the primary objective explicitly weights delivery risk alongside cost. I'm treating this as a standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout — commit to the new vendor for the contract term but build in tight monitoring and a fallback trigger, since a no-buffer line can't absorb an onboarding hiccup the way the archived precedent's context might have allowed. This is flagged as carrying downstream value risk because switching primary supply with zero volume slack is inherently more fragile than the precedent suggests, and I'm preserving uncertainty rather than treating memory_c2's 'quick, clean' outcome as guaranteed to repeat under today's tighter operating margin.
